Description: A diverse urban constituency centred on Peterborough, a post-war expanded city with a major manufacturing, logistics and distribution economy. It has a particularly large South Asian population, especially Pakistani, alongside substantial eastern european migration

Name: Poole
Description: A large coastal town west of Bournemouth built around a major harbour, with tourism, banking and freight shipping as key industries. Long one of the more affluent Dorset seats, with high owner-occupation.

Name: Portsmouth North
Description: Covering the northern part of Portsea Island and mainland suburbs such as Cosham and Drayton, this Portsmouth seat is largely white and working-class. Paulsgrove, a large council estate, is among the most deprived areas, contrasting with more settled owner-occupied areas elsewhere.

Name: Portsmouth South
Description: A dense, historic naval constituency at the southern tip of Portsea Island, home to the Royal Navy dockyard, HMS Victory and the seaside resort of Southsea. The University of Portsmouth gives it a large student population, and it is markedly more diverse and transient than Portsmouth North.

Name: Rushcliffe
Description: An affluent suburban and rural constituency south of Nottingham, centred on West Bridgford and extending into prosperous villages and market towns. It has an exceptionally high level of owner occupation, degree holders and professional employment, with a highly educated, settled population and very little social housing. Many residents commute into Nottingham, while agriculture remains important in its rural areas.

Name: Salisbury
Description: A cathedral city with a large military hospital as its biggest employer, taking in the village of Wilton, once famous for carpet-making, and the market town of Tisbury. An affluent, well-qualified and historic seat near the Dorset border.

Name: Sheffield Central
Description: Sheffield's city centre and inner-west, including the regenerated Kelham Island area and university district. An exceptionally young, highly educated, private-renting seat with one of the largest Chinese populations in the country.

Name: Skipton and Ripon
Description: A large, rural North Yorkshire seat of dales, moorland and market towns, centred on Skipton and the small cathedral city of Ripon. An affluent, elderly and overwhelmingly white seat reliant on tourism and sheep farming.

Name: South Derbyshire
Description: Combining industrial Swadlincote with growing commuter villages south of Derby. While manufacturing, logistics and employment connected to the Derby economy remain important. Its high level of owner occupation gives much of the constituency a settled suburban character.

Name: South Devon
Description: Covers the yachting towns of Dartmouth and Salcombe and the alternative-minded town of Totnes, along with the fishing port of Brixham. A wealthy, elderly seat reliant on tourism, fishing and small business.

Name: South Norfolk
Description: A rural constituency of villages and small towns south and west of Norwich, centred on Diss and the fast-growing town of Wymondham, also home to Lotus's car plant. Many residents commute into Norwich or work in its hospitals and public services, and it has one of the highest owner-occupation rates in the country and a notably elderly population.

Name: South Northamptonshire
Description: A predominantly rural and affluent constituency of market towns, villages and expanding commuter settlements between Northampton, Milton Keynes and Oxford. High levels of professional employment and home ownership give it a prosperous, settled character, while strong road and rail connections have encouraged substantial population growth

Name: South Suffolk
Description: A rural Suffolk constituency centred on the wool towns of Sudbury and Lavenham, taking in villages along the Stour valley known as Constable Country. It has an unusually elderly population and a strong agricultural and small-manufacturing base.

Name: South West Wiltshire
Description: Centred on the county town of Trowbridge along with Warminster and Westbury, with Salisbury Plain and its military ranges - including the abandoned village of Imber - to the east. A settled, largely white and rural constituency with a strong army presence around Warminster.

Name: Southampton Itchen
Description: The eastern half of Southampton across the River Itchen, including the former shipbuilding area of Woolston and the redeveloped Ocean Village waterfront. It is more working-class and ethnically homogeneous than neighbouring Southampton Test, with an older population.

Name: Southampton Test
Description: The western half of Southampton, taking in the university campus at Portswood and the residential wards of Shirley and Millbrook. It has a young, studenty population and is more ethnically diverse than its Itchen neighbour across the river.

Name: Stevenage
Description: One of Britain's original post-war New Towns, Stevenage was purpose-built from 1946 with distinct residential neighbourhoods around a pedestrianised centre, and takes in the nearby villages of Knebworth and Codicote. Its demographic profile sits close to the national average on almost every measure.

Name: Stockton West
Description: A more affluent Teesside seat spanning both banks of the Tees, including the private new town of Ingleby Barwick and the historic market town of Yarm. It has one of the highest owner-occupation rates in the country.

Name: Stroud
Description: The Stroud Valleys, a former textile-milling district in Gloucestershire, running from Dursley and Stonehouse through Cotswold villages to Wotton-under-Edge. Known for a strong alternative and nonconformist culture alongside continuing manufacturing employment.

Name: Suffolk Coastal
Description: A largely rural and coastal Suffolk constituency stretching from the container port of Felixstowe to the genteel resort towns of Aldeburgh, known for its music festival, and Woodbridge, with the long-vanished medieval port of Dunwich in between. Away from the port, the seat has an unusually elderly population.

Name: Taunton and Wellington
Description: Somerset's county town, home to major public-sector employers including the county council and a large hospital, alongside the smaller town of Wellington, known for its public school. Takes in villages in the Quantock and Blackdown Hills.

Name: Tewkesbury
Description: A prosperous, historic market town in northern Gloucestershire, taking in Bishop's Cleeve and the northern edges of Cheltenham and Gloucester, plus Cheltenham Racecourse. A well-off, commuter-oriented seat with a strong farming tradition.

Name: Tottenham
Description: One of Britain's most ethnically diverse constituencies, Tottenham has large Black, Turkish, Kurdish, Greek-Cypriot and African communities. Historically associated with deprivation and social housing, the area has seen increasing regeneration and gentrification around Tottenham Hale. The constituency has played an important role in London's multicultural history. Rates of private and social renting are very high, whilst homeownership is very low.

Name: Truro and Falmouth
Description: Pairs Cornwall's county town, Truro, a former tin-mining port, with the university town and port of Falmouth beneath Pendennis Castle. A growing student population and public-sector employment shape the seat's character.

Name: Walthamstow
Description: Once a traditional working-class East London suburb, Walthamstow has become one of London's best-known centres of gentrification. Young professionals have been drawn by good transport links, while the constituency retains a diverse population and strong East End identity. Walthamstow Village provides a distinctive historic contrast to the surrounding urban neighbourhoods.

Name: Warrington South
Description: The more affluent, 'true Cheshire' half of Warrington new town, including Appleton, Stockton Heath and Grappenhall south of the Manchester Ship Canal. Higher home ownership and qualifications than its northern counterpart, with rugby league a strong local tradition.

Name: Waveney Valley
Description: A new constituency created in the 2024 boundary changes, straddling the Norfolk-Suffolk border and taking in Bungay, Harleston, Diss and the small town of Eye, once its own parliamentary seat. Overwhelmingly rural and elderly, it has one of the smallest populations of young adults and children in the country.

Name: Weald of Kent
Description: A newly created, affluent rural Kent seat of market towns and villages such as Tenterden and Cranbrook, with extensive woodland and orchards. It has a notably elderly population and includes Sissinghurst Castle Gardens.

Name: Wells and Mendip Hills
Description: A rural Somerset seat spanning the Somerset Levels and the Mendip Hills, including Cheddar Gorge and Wookey Hole, with Wells - England's smallest city - and Shepton Mallet as its main towns. Also home to the Glastonbury Festival site at Pilton; notably elderly and affluent.

Name: West Dorset
Description: Dorset's largest constituency by area, covering the Jurassic Coast and taking in Dorchester, Bridport and the seaside town of Lyme Regis. A notably elderly, rural seat with little heavy industry.

Name: Wetherby and Easingwold
Description: A patchwork rural seat stretching from prosperous Leeds suburbs and the racing town of Wetherby to North Yorkshire market towns like Tadcaster, known for its breweries, and Easingwold. An affluent, well-qualified and overwhelmingly white seat built on agriculture and equestrian interests.

Name: Worthing West
Description: The western part of the seaside resort of Worthing, extending into nearby coastal villages. Traditionally a retirement destination, it has recently seen an influx of younger residents drawn by relatively affordable housing and a large private-rented sector.

Name: Wythenshawe and Sale East
Description: Sharply contrasts the middle-class commuter suburb of Sale with Wythenshawe, once Europe's largest council estate, split by Manchester Airport. Sale has high qualifications and home ownership; Wythenshawe has substantial social housing and lower incomes.

Name: Yeovil
Description: A south Somerset seat centred on the market town of Yeovil, historically known for glove-making and now for helicopter manufacturing, taking in Chard, Crewkerne and Ilminster to the west. A fairly typical rural and small-town constituency.

Name: Aberafan Maesteg
Description: A working-class South Wales seat centred on the steel town of Port Talbot, once home to Britain's largest steelworks, and the former mining valley town of Maesteg. It has low qualification levels and a strong industrial heritage, and produced actors Richard Burton and Anthony Hopkins.

Name: Aberdeenshire North and Moray East
Description: A rural, coastal seat along Scotland's northeast, taking in fishing ports such as Peterhead, Fraserburgh and Buckie that still land nearly half of all Scottish fish catches. Over 40% of residents speak the Doric dialect, and prosperous farming villages sit alongside more deprived fishing communities.

Name: Airdrie and Shotts
Description: A central Scotland seat combining the town of Airdrie with smaller communities including Shotts, on the M8 corridor east of Glasgow. Once dependent on weaving, coal and iron, it now relies on light industry and logistics, with a notably mixed religious make-up for the area.

Name: Aldridge-Brownhills
Description: A Walsall borough seat combining the former mining town of Brownhills with the more affluent, suburban areas of Aldridge and Streetly, on Birmingham's northern fringe. It has a high rate of home ownership and a working-class character, with comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Alloa and Grangemouth
Description: An oddly-shaped Central Scotland seat split by the Firth of Forth, combining Clackmannanshire towns like Alloa with the industrial town of Grangemouth, home to Scotland's only oil refinery. A working-class seat with a strong heritage in coal, textiles and brewing.

Name: Alyn and Deeside
Description: An industrial North Wales seat along the Dee estuary, dominated by steelworks and heavy industry around Connah's Quay and Shotton. It is the least Welsh-born constituency in Wales, reflecting its close ties to nearby England.

Name: Amber Valley
Description: A mixed constituency of former coal-mining towns such as Ripley and Heanor alongside more affluent villages and commuter communities. The area's economy has shifted from coal and heavy industry towards manufacturing, logistics and commuting to Derby and Nottingham.

Name: Angus and Perthshire Glens
Description: A large rural seat of glens, mountains and farmland north of Dundee, taking in the towns of Forfar, Montrose and Brechin as well as the tourist resorts of Pitlochry and Aberfeldy. J.M. Barrie's birthplace of Kirriemuir lies within the seat, which has an older, largely owner-occupied population.

Name: Arbroath and Broughty Ferry
Description: Northeast of Dundee, running from the affluent seaside suburb of Broughty Ferry to the fishing port of Arbroath, famous for its smoked haddock, and the golfing town of Carnoustie. Combines Dundee's post-war housing estates with wealthier coastal Angus towns.

Name: Argyll, Bute and South Lochaber
Description: A vast, sparsely populated Highland and island seat covering Argyll and Bute, including the islands of Islay, Mull and Bute, plus remote mainland areas like Ardnamurchan. Farming, fishing, whisky distilling and tourism dominate, and ferry links are a defining feature of daily life.

Name: Ashfield
Description: A former Nottinghamshire coalfield constituency centred on Sutton-in-Ashfield and Kirkby-in-Ashfield. Characterised by working-class communities, very low levels of higher education and a strong post-industrial identity.

Name: Ashton-under-Lyne
Description: A working-class Tameside town east of Manchester, with a textile-industry past and a large Asian population concentrated in the town centre, contrasting with the more settled, largely white suburbs of Droylsden, Audenshaw and Dukinfield. Educational attainment is well below average.

Name: Ayr, Carrick and Cumnock
Description: Combines the seaside town of Ayr with rural Carrick to the south and former mining communities around Cumnock to the east. Golf tourism thrives around Turnberry, while ex-mining towns like New Cumnock remain among the more deprived parts of Ayrshire, and Robert Burns was born nearby in Alloway.

Name: Bangor Aberconwy
Description: A North Wales coastal seat combining the seaside resort of Llandudno with the university city of Bangor, where students make up a large share of the population. Inland, English-speaking coastal towns give way to more mountainous, Welsh-speaking communities.

Name: Barnsley North
Description: Part of the old South Yorkshire coalfield, taking in Barnsley town and former mining villages such as Grimethorpe, setting for the film Brassed Off. A settled, overwhelmingly white and working-class seat, with low rates of higher education.

Name: Barnsley South
Description: Another former South Yorkshire coalfield seat, combining Barnsley's southern suburbs with ex-mining towns such as Wombwell, Goldthorpe and Thurnscoe. A working-class, overwhelmingly white seat with some of the lowest qualification levels and highest deprivation in the country.

Name: Barrow and Furness
Description: An isolated shipbuilding town on the Furness peninsula, cut off from the rest of Cumbria by Morecambe Bay, with BAE Systems' naval shipyard dominating the local economy. The seat also takes in rural Furness countryside and Walney Island's beaches, and is overwhelmingly white British.

Name: Bassetlaw
Description: A geographically varied constituency centred on Worksop and Retford. Once dominated by coal mining, it now combines former pit communities with market towns and productive agricultural land close to South Yorkshire.

Name: Bathgate and Linlithgow
Description: A West Lothian seat of former mining and manufacturing towns - Bathgate, Whitburn, Armadale and Bo'ness - between Edinburgh and Glasgow, alongside the historic royal burgh of Linlithgow. Industries from shale oil to car and jeans manufacturing have come and gone, leaving a settled, working-class character.

Name: Bedford
Description: A diverse constituency with sizeable black, asian, and a historical Italian community. The local economy is based around public services, education, retail, logistics and professional employment, while Bedford's rail connections also support commuting towards London.

Name: Berwickshire, Roxburgh and Selkirk
Description: The Scottish Borders, taking in textile towns like Hawick and Galashiels, historically known for tweed and cashmere, plus smaller towns including Kelso, Melrose and Jedburgh. A rural, agricultural seat and home to Sir Walter Scott's house at Abbotsford.

Name: Beverley and Holderness
Description: Combines the historic market town of Beverley, home to a famous medieval minster, with the flat farmland and seaside towns of Holderness, including Withernsea and Hornsea. An affluent, elderly and overwhelmingly white seat, with a more deprived, tourism-reliant coastal fringe.

Name: Birkenhead
Description: A Mersey-side town facing Liverpool, built on a now-declined shipbuilding and docks economy, taking in Oxton, Tranmere and Rock Ferry. It has a strong Victorian terraced housing stock, a distinct identity from Liverpool across the water, and below-average qualifications.

Name: Birmingham Erdington
Description: A working-class North Birmingham seat combining the inter-war council estate of Kingstanding with the redeveloped Castle Vale estate. It has a diverse population, with significant Black and South Asian communities, and comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Birmingham Hall Green and Moseley
Description: A diverse, inner South Birmingham seat spanning affluent, leafy Moseley and the historic Muslim-majority area of Sparkbrook, one of only two such seats in Britain. It combines a large South Asian population with pockets of severe deprivation.

Name: Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North
Description: A sharply divided seat combining Muslim-majority inner Birmingham areas like Alum Rock with white, middle-class peripheral estates and the separate, historic suburb of Castle Bromwich. It has some of the lowest graduate rates and professional employment in the country.

Name: Birmingham Northfield
Description: A working-class South West Birmingham seat built around the former Longbridge car plant, alongside more affluent Northfield and peripheral estates at Frankley and Rubery. Graduate rates and professional employment are below average.

Name: Birmingham Perry Barr
Description: A diverse, working-class North Birmingham seat combining the inner-city areas of Handsworth and Aston with the more suburban Perry Barr and Oscott. It has a large South Asian population, with substantial Muslim and Sikh communities, and one of the country's least white constituencies.

Name: Birmingham Selly Oak
Description: A varied South Birmingham seat spanning the student area around the university, the model Quaker-built estate of Bournville, and more working-class Billesley and Druids Heath. It has a large student population and an otherwise fairly average demographic profile.

Name: Birmingham Yardley
Description: A working-class South East Birmingham seat taking in Small Heath, with its large Muslim community, alongside more suburban and affluent Sheldon. Graduate rates and professional employment are below average.

Name: Bishop Auckland
Description: A large, mostly rural former Durham coalfield seat stretching from the Tees and Wear valleys into Pennine hill country. Bishop Auckland itself grew from mining and ironworking into a market town around Auckland Castle, once the Bishop of Durham's palace. It has a strongly white, working-class population with below-average qualifications.

Name: Blackburn
Description: A former cotton-mill town in Lancashire with a very large South Asian, predominantly Muslim population - one of the highest shares in the country - and comparatively low qualifications and incomes. Blackburn Rovers' football ground remains a focal point of local identity.

Name: Blackley and Middleton South
Description: A mix of deprived inner-Manchester wards (Harpurhey, Collyhurst, Crumpsall) and more affluent Rochdale suburbs such as Alkrington Garden Village, split by the M60. Heaton Park, one of the largest municipal parks in Europe, dominates the north of the seat.

Name: Blackpool North and Fleetwood
Description: The quieter, more suburban northern end of the Blackpool seafront, taking in Bispham and Norbreck, together with the separate fishing and industrial town of Fleetwood. An elderly, overwhelmingly white population with below-average qualifications.

Name: Blackpool South
Description: Covers Blackpool's central seafront and Golden Mile tourist strip - home to the Tower, Pleasure Beach and faded seaside guesthouses - along with dense residential streets behind it. One of the most deprived seats in the country, with high private renting and low qualifications.

Name: Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney
Description: Two South Wales valleys built on iron and coal, including Ebbw Vale and Tredegar, now among the most post-industrial and deprived seats in Britain. Qualification levels are low and long-term illness is common, a legacy of the area's mining past.

Name: Blaydon and Consett
Description: A former coal-mining and steel constituency northwest of Durham, combining Blaydon - including Chopwell, noted for its socialist-era street names - with the ex-steel town of Consett. It has a strongly white, working-class population with below-average qualifications.

Name: Blyth and Ashington
Description: A post-industrial Northumberland seat covering the former mining towns of Ashington, Blyth and Bedlington, once among the country's largest coalfields. Blyth retains a working port, but the wider area has one of the lowest graduate rates in England and a settled, overwhelmingly white population.

Name: Bognor Regis and Littlehampton
Description: A West Sussex seaside constituency combining the resort towns of Bognor Regis and Littlehampton with surrounding coastal villages. It has one of the most elderly populations in the country and a strong retirement and tourism character.

Name: Bolsover
Description: One of Britain's classic former coalfield constituencies, centred on Bolsover, Shirebrook and surrounding ex-mining villages. The area retains a strong working-class identity despite the decline of mining, with warehousing and manufacturing now major employers.

Name: Bolton North East
Description: A sharply polarised Bolton seat, combining working-class, largely Pakistani-Muslim inner wards such as Halliwell with the affluent commuter suburbs of Bromley Cross and Bradshaw. Built on a cotton-manufacturing past - Samuel Crompton invented the spinning mule here.

Name: Bolton South and Walkden
Description: Takes in Farnworth, Kearsley, Little Hulton and Walkden across Bolton and Salford, an area built on coal, cotton and chemicals. It has a substantial Muslim population and below-average qualifications, and is home to one of the country's largest Tesco stores.

Name: Bolton West
Description: Combines affluent Bolton suburbs such as Heaton and Smithills with the former mill and mining town of Westhoughton and the railway town of Horwich. A settled, largely white, home-owning seat with above-average professional employment.

Name: Bootle
Description: A dockland area on Liverpool's northern edge, taking in Litherland, Waterloo and Seaforth, historically among the most deprived parts of Merseyside. It has an unusually high Christian population and close-knit, extended-family communities with little outward commuting.

Name: Boston and Skegness
Description: Combining the market town of Boston with the seaside resort of Skegness, this constituency has one of the UK's largest agricultural sectors and significant food processing industries. It has experienced substantial Eastern European migration since the 2000s. especially in Boston Town itself, and voted heavily to leave the EU.

Name: Bradford East
Description: Northern and eastern Bradford, from Victorian inner-city wards to the more middle-class suburb of Idle and Thackley. A young, ethnically diverse seat with a large Muslim population and high deprivation.

Name: Bradford South
Description: Southern Bradford, combining the working-class core around Wibsey with the outlying Pennine village of Queensbury and rural Tong. A working-class seat with lower qualifications and, compared to other Bradford seats, a smaller Muslim population.

Name: Bradford West
Description: Central and western Bradford, from the Victorian core around Manningham to Pennine fringe villages such as Clayton and Thornton. England's most Muslim constituency, with a large Pakistani community, high deprivation and low rates of professional employment.

Name: Braintree
Description: Rural Essex constituency centred on Braintree and smaller towns such as Halstead and surrounding villages. Traditionally associated with manufacturing, the area now has a more mixed economy of retail, logistics and commuting

Name: Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe
Description: A large, sparsely populated Mid Wales seat combining the Brecon Beacons and spa towns such as Llandrindod Wells with former mining valleys added from Neath. It has an unusually high rate of self-employment and a strong agricultural base.

Name: Bridgend
Description: A South Wales seat combining the town of Bridgend with the seaside resort of Porthcawl, historically home to a large wartime munitions factory and, more recently, a Ford engine plant. Its demographic profile is fairly average for Wales, neither especially affluent nor deprived.

Name: Bridgwater
Description: A working-class Somerset town historically built around a cellophane factory, now taking in the seaside commuter town of Burnham-on-Sea. Inter-war council estates sit alongside more affluent western suburbs.

Name: Bridlington and The Wolds
Description: Combines the seaside resort of Bridlington and Hornsea with the rolling chalk farmland of the Yorkshire Wolds. An elderly, overwhelmingly white and rural seat reliant on tourism and agriculture, with below-average qualifications.

Name: Brigg and Immingham
Description: A largely rural North Lincolnshire seat centred on the port town of Immingham and the small market town of Brigg, taking in Wolds villages and Grimsby's commuter suburbs. An overwhelmingly white, older seat with high home ownership and comparatively low qualification levels.

Name: Bristol East
Description: Spans both banks of the River Avon, from the diverse, multicultural inner-city wards of Easton and Lawrence Hill to the more homogeneous suburban areas of Brislington and Stockwood. Much of the seat grew out of the old east Bristol coalfield.

Name: Bristol North East
Description: Combining older, working-class areas of Bristol such as Eastville and Lockleaze with the former mining town of Kingswood in South Gloucestershire. A mixed suburban seat of council estates and inter-war housing.

Name: Bristol South
Description: The most suburban of Bristol's seats, covering the southern edge of the city from gentrified inner areas like Southville to outer council estates such as Hartcliffe and Withywood. More working-class and ethnically homogeneous than the rest of Bristol.

Name: Broadland and Fakenham
Description: Rural cosntituency combining Commuter Villages North of Norwich to the market town of Fakenham. Agriculture and food production remain important, and The constituency has an older, settled and strongly homeowner-dominated population.

Name: Bromsgrove
Description: An affluent Worcestershire seat combining the town of Bromsgrove, historically a nail-making centre, with commuter villages toward Birmingham and the Lickey and Clent Hills. It has high rates of home ownership and professional employment.

Name: Broxtowe
Description: A suburban constituency west of Nottingham, including Beeston, Stapleford and former mining communities such as Eastwood. It combines university-linked professional communities with traditional industrial towns and commuter suburbs.

Name: Burnley
Description: A former cotton town on Lancashire's 'cotton thread' of mill towns, with a significant Asian population well above the regional average and comparatively low qualifications and incomes. Manufacturing decline has left the seat among the most deprived in the country.

Name: Burton and Uttoxeter
Description: A Staffordshire seat combining the brewing town of Burton-on-Trent, historically home to Bass and Marston's, with the market town of Uttoxeter and rural villages toward the Peak District. It has an average, fairly working-class demographic profile.

Name: Bury North
Description: Covers the northern half of Bury borough, including Ramsbottom and Tottington, an area of former paper and textile mills now relatively affluent by Greater Manchester standards. Bury Market and the heritage East Lancashire Railway are local landmarks.

Name: Caerfyrddin
Description: A largely rural, Welsh-speaking Carmarthenshire seat with no large towns, taking in Ammanford, Llandeilo and Llandovery. It has a notably elderly population and a strong farming tradition.

Name: Caerphilly
Description: A former mining seat in the lower Rhymney Valley centred on the market town of Caerphilly, home to one of Britain's largest medieval castles and the cheese once made locally, now produced in England. Its ex-mining communities give it a strongly working-class character.

Name: Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross
Description: The UK's largest constituency by area, stretching from Britain's northernmost point at Dunnet Head across the vast Flow Country peatlands. Historically dependent on fishing and agriculture, with tourism now boosted by the North Coast 500 route; an elderly, sparsely populated seat with pockets of deprivation in towns like Wick and Thurso.

Name: Calder Valley
Description: A Pennine West Yorkshire seat combining old mill towns in the steep Calder valley, including the increasingly gentrified Hebden Bridge, with the flatter towns of Elland and Brighouse to the east. A relatively affluent, professional seat known for its progressive, alternative character around Hebden Bridge.

Name: Camborne and Redruth
Description: Twin former mining towns in Cornwall, built on tin and copper extraction that collapsed with the closure of South Crofty mine, now reliant on small businesses. Also takes in the port town of Hayle.

Name: Cannock Chase
Description: A former coal-mining district in Staffordshire, centred on the towns of Cannock and Rugeley, with surrounding heathland. It has a strongly working-class character and comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Cardiff East
Description: The eastern side of the Welsh capital, spanning affluent suburbs such as Cyncoed and Roath alongside more deprived inner-city and 1960s estate areas like Trowbridge and Llanrumney. It has a young, ethnically mixed population.

Name: Cardiff North
Description: An affluent, mostly suburban seat in north Cardiff, taking in Lisvane, Rhiwbina and Llanishen. It has high owner-occupation, a well-qualified, professional population and a large commuter base into the city centre.

Name: Cardiff South and Penarth
Description: Cardiff's waterfront seat, taking in the redeveloped Cardiff Bay and Senedd alongside working-class inner-city areas like Butetown and Grangetown, plus the genteel Victorian seaside town of Penarth. Once a major coal-exporting port, it now has a young, ethnically diverse population with a large student presence.

Name: Cardiff West
Description: Cardiff's western side, running from the diverse inner-city Riverside area through gentrifying Canton and Pontcanna to more deprived former council estates at Ely and Caerau, and affluent northern villages near St Fagans. It has an unusually young population for a British seat.

Name: Carlisle
Description: Cumbria's only city, a former Roman garrison and mill town that now anchors a wide rural hinterland including Brampton and Longtown. It has a large student population from the University of Cumbria and is overwhelmingly white.

Name: Castle Point
Description: Suburban Coastal Essex constituency characterised by very high levels of home ownership, very low levels of social housing, very low levels of further education and high levels of self employment and skilled manual labour occupations.

Name: Central Ayrshire
Description: Combines the former new town of Irvine with the golfing and coastal towns of Troon and Prestwick. A mixed seat contrasting Irvine's working-class character with the more affluent, service-based economy of its neighbours.

Name: Ceredigion Preseli
Description: A rural, coastal Mid Wales seat taking in Aberystwyth and Cardigan, with a strong Welsh-speaking majority and a large student population thanks to Aberystwyth and Lampeter's universities. Tourism, agriculture and the Fishguard ferry port support the local economy.

Name: Chatham and Aylesford
Description: An odd, barbell-shaped Kent seat combining the working-class naval town of Chatham with the more rural, modest villages of Aylesford and Snodland to the south. It has a lower rate of degree qualifications than most of the South East.

Name: Chesterfield
Description: A historic Derbyshire market town and former coalfield constituency. Chesterfield remains an important retail and service centre for North Derbyshire, with its famous crooked spire and surrounding former mining communities shaping its identity.

Name: Chorley
Description: A Lancashire market town with substantial rural surroundings, including the elevated moorland of Rivington and Winter Hill, and newer developments like Buckshaw Village on a former munitions site. An ageing, overwhelmingly white and largely home-owning population.

Name: Christchurch
Description: A Dorset seaside seat taking in the historic town of Christchurch and East Dorset commuter settlements such as Ferndown. One of the oldest and most home-owning constituencies in the country, with Bournemouth Airport nearby.

Name: City of Durham
Description: Centred on the cathedral city of Durham, home to Durham University and a large student population, surrounded by former coal-mining villages such as Bowburn and Brandon. It combines a historic, well-educated core with a more working-class coalfield hinterland.

Name: Clacton
Description: Deprived Coastal Essex constitueny comprising the seaside resort of Clacton and surrounding towns. These include Jaywick, the most deprived Neighbourhood in England. Rates of higher education are very low, whilst the median age is very high

Name: Clwyd East
Description: A North Wales seat running from the seaside resort of Prestatyn through the county town of Mold to Llangollen. It is notably elderly and affluent for the region, combining industrial Flint with retiree-heavy coastal towns and rural farmland.

Name: Clwyd North
Description: A North Wales coastal seat stretching from the seaside towns of Rhyl and Colwyn Bay - the former among the most deprived areas in Wales - to more affluent inland towns such as Denbigh, where the Welsh language remains stronger.

Name: Coatbridge and Bellshill
Description: A former industrial area east of Glasgow, once dominated by ironworks, now relying on its location between Glasgow and Edinburgh for light industry, retail and logistics. It has Scotland's largest Catholic population and hosts the country's biggest St Patrick's Day celebrations.

Name: Colne Valley
Description: A Pennine seat around Huddersfield combining the mill towns of the Colne and Holme valleys, including Marsden and Holmfirth, the setting for Last of the Summer Wine, with western Huddersfield suburbs. A more middle-class, well-educated seat than much of West Yorkshire, with a strong textile heritage.

Name: Congleton
Description: A rural southeast Cheshire seat of small towns including Congleton, Sandbach and Alsager, with a manufacturing history in silk, lorries and, more recently, airbags and golf balls. Affluent, elderly and overwhelmingly white, with the Jodrell Bank telescope visible on the horizon.

Name: Corby and East Northamptonshire
Description: A constituency combining the rapidly growing town of Corby with surrounding market towns and rural villages. Corby has a distinctive Scottish heritage due to its steel industry and today has a large manufacturing, logistics and distribution sector.

Name: Coventry North West
Description: Combining Coventry's more affluent western suburbs with the deprived inner areas of Radford and Holbrook, plus a slice of surrounding greenbelt. It has a mixed population, with Sikh and Muslim communities concentrated in its more working-class wards.

Name: Cowdenbeath and Kirkcaldy
Description: Fife coastal towns including Kirkcaldy and Cowdenbeath, both shaped by coal mining and, in Kirkcaldy's case, linoleum manufacturing. Now a more diversified service economy, with retail parks and public-sector employment, alongside the birthplaces of economist Adam Smith and architect Robert Adam.

Name: Cramlington and Killingworth
Description: Former Northumberland and North Tyneside coalfield country, combining the planned towns of Cramlington and Killingworth - both now largely middle-class commuter settlements for Newcastle - with more deprived ex-mining villages. Owner-occupation is high and the population is overwhelmingly white.

Name: Crewe and Nantwich
Description: Contrasts the railway town of Crewe, built almost entirely around its works and now more diverse and deprived, with the affluent, historic market town of Nantwich and its half-timbered centre. Rolls-Royce and Bentley have long been major local employers.

Name: Cumbernauld and Kirkintilloch
Description: The new town of Cumbernauld, built from 1955, together with the older industrial town of Kilsyth and part of Kirkintilloch. A mostly working-class seat with high home ownership, contrasting Cumbernauld's planned estates with Kilsyth's more traditional character.

Name: Dagenham and Rainham
Description: Centred on the former Ford manufacturing heartland of Dagenham, this constituency combines working-class East London with the more suburban communities of Rainham. Once one of London's least diverse areas, it has experienced rapid demographic change alongside extensive new rental housing developments.

Name: Darlington
Description: A former railway town - birthplace of the world's first public passenger railway - now reliant on administrative offices, warehousing and engineering firms after its locomotive works and textile mills closed. It has a marked divide between more affluent western suburbs and poorer eastern wards.

Name: Derbyshire Dales
Description: A predominantly rural constituency covering much of the Peak District National Park. Tourism, agriculture and market towns such as Bakewell and Matlock dominate the local economy, alongside affluent villages and attractive retirement communities.

Name: Dewsbury and Batley
Description: A West Yorkshire seat in the old 'Heavy Woollen District', historically built on recycled wool textiles. Dewsbury and Batley have large, long-established South Asian communities, and the seat has a substantial Muslim population alongside high deprivation.

Name: Doncaster Central
Description: Covers Doncaster's town centre and southern suburbs, from council estates to the more middle-class Tickhill and Bessacarr. Built on the railway industry - the Flying Scotsman and Mallard locomotives were built here - the seat has high deprivation in its central wards.

Name: Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme
Description: Combines former mining towns east of Doncaster, including Thorne and Hatfield, with the flat, rural Isle of Axholme across the Lincolnshire border. A working-class, ageing seat with a mining heritage, though parts of the Isle of Axholme are more prosperous.

Name: Doncaster North
Description: Combines former mining towns such as Stainforth, Mexborough and Bentley with more affluent rural villages like Sprotbrough. A working-class seat with a strong mining heritage and below-average qualifications.

Name: Dover and Deal
Description: Kent's historic Channel port, centred on Dover beneath the White Cliffs, and the seaside town of Deal, with former mining villages inland from the old Kent coalfield. It has a working-class character and below-average qualifications.

Name: Dudley
Description: The historic 'capital of the Black Country', built on coal and iron and centred on its medieval castle. It has a strongly working-class character with comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Dumfries and Galloway
Description: A rural south-west Scotland seat spanning the Galloway Forest and Southern Uplands, with the port town of Stranraer serving ferries to Belfast. Dumfries itself has pockets of both significant deprivation and affluence, and farming remains central to the wider economy.

Name: Dumfriesshire, Clydesdale and Tweeddale
County: Dumfries and Galloway; Scottish Borders; South Lanarkshire
Description: A large South of Scotland seat bordering England, taking in the spa towns of Peebles and Moffat, the market town of Biggar and Gretna Green at the border crossing. Rural and affluent, with agriculture and a legacy of textile and coal industries.

Name: Dundee Central
Description: The heart of Dundee, including the university, football grounds and West End tenements. Once built on jute manufacturing, the city has diversified, with a young, studentified population and significant public-sector employment.

Name: Dunfermline and Dollar
Description: Scotland's ancient former capital, Dunfermline, granted city status in 2022, together with the port of Rosyth and the town of Dollar in Clackmannanshire. Once built on linen mills, the local economy now includes major employers such as Amazon.

Name: Dunstable and Leighton Buzzard
Description: Combines the Luton suburbs of Dunstable and Houghton Regis with the affluent Commuter town of Leighton Buzzard. Located between Milton Keynes and London, the area has seen significant population growth and extensive housing development.

Name: Dwyfor Meirionnydd
Description: A mountainous North West Wales seat taking in Snowdonia, Caernarfon and the former slate town of Blaenau Ffestiniog. It has one of the highest proportions of Welsh speakers in the country, alongside a large elderly and second-home-owning population, and relies heavily on tourism.

Name: Easington
Description: A former County Durham coalfield seat combining old pit villages with the planned New Town of Peterlee, built for miners in the post-war decades. It has a strongly working-class, overwhelmingly white population and notably poor health outcomes.

Name: East Kilbride and Strathaven
Description: Scotland's oldest new town, East Kilbride, combined with the market town of Strathaven and former weaving town of Stonehouse. Manufacturing and office employment anchor the local economy, alongside a settled, largely owner-occupied population.

Name: East Renfrewshire
Description: One of Scotland's most affluent seats, combining the well-off Glasgow suburbs of Newton Mearns, Giffnock and Clarkston with the more working-class town of Barrhead. Home to a significant Jewish and Muslim population, alongside high rates of professional employment and home ownership.

Name: East Thanet
Description: The eastern part of the Isle of Thanet, taking in the seaside towns of Ramsgate and Broadstairs and part of Margate. A traditional but declining resort economy has left it more working-class and higher-renting than most of the South East.

Name: East Worthing and Shoreham
Description: A Sussex coastal seat combining Shoreham, with its boat harbour and small airfield, and the eastern part of Worthing. It has an elderly, largely owner-occupying population and a mix of dormitory and retirement housing.

Name: Eastleigh
Description: A Victorian railway town north of Southampton, taking in the commuter suburbs of Chandler's Ford and Fair Oak. It has a solidly middle-class, owner-occupying character with pockets of social housing.

Name: Ellesmere Port and Bromborough
Description: An industrial seat at the foot of the Wirral, dominated by the Stanlow oil refinery, a large Vauxhall car plant, docks and chemical works. Despite comparatively high home ownership, it has a strong working-class, Merseyside-oriented character.

Name: Erewash
Description: Centred on Ilkeston and Long Eaton, this constituency combines former industrial towns with commuter communities between Derby and Nottingham. Manufacturing remains important alongside logistics and service industries.

Name: Erith and Thamesmead
Description: A working-class Thameside constituency with extensive post-war housing estates and one of the highest proportions of social housing in England. It has a large and growing Black population - among the highest of any UK constituency - as well as significant ethnic diversity resulting from recent demographic change.

Name: Falkirk
Description: An old ironworking town in Scotland's Central Belt, now known for the Falkirk Wheel boat lift and the Kelpies sculptures. A working-class seat with a strong canal heritage, sitting between Edinburgh and Stirling.

Name: Forest of Dean
Description: A wooded, once heavily industrial constituency in western Gloucestershire, built on coal mining and iron working and still home to a handful of traditional 'freeminers'. Centred on Cinderford, Coleford and Lydney, near the Welsh border.

Name: Gainsborough
Description: A largely rural Lincolnshire constituency centred on the market town of Gainsborough. Agriculture and food production are major industries, while the constituency also includes numerous villages and small market towns with an ageing population.

Name: Gateshead Central and Whickham
Description: Covering most of the industrial town of Gateshead, immediately south of Newcastle, together with the more suburban former mining area of Whickham and the Metrocentre shopping complex. It has a small but notable Orthodox Jewish community in Bensham.

Name: Gedling
Description: A suburban constituency north east of Nottingham, combining commuter suburbs with former Nottinghamshire coalfield communities such as Arnold, Carlton and Netherfield. It has become increasingly residential as mining has disappeared.

Name: Gillingham and Rainham
Description: A Medway towns seat combining Gillingham, with its terraced housing and football club, and the more suburban, owner-occupied Rainham to the east. It has a growing Black population and a fairly even social mix.

Name: Glasgow East
Description: Glasgow's East End, from the cathedral and Glasgow Green out to Shettleston and Baillieston. Once an industrial powerhouse for engineering and textiles, it remains one of the city's more deprived areas despite ongoing regeneration.

Name: Glasgow North East
Description: Northeast Glasgow, cut off from the rest of the city by the motorway network, taking in Springburn, Easterhouse and Barlinnie Prison. Once centred on locomotive and chemical manufacturing, it remains one of Scotland's most deprived seats, though areas like Dennistoun have gentrified rapidly.

Name: Glasgow South
Description: The city's southside, from grand tenements and mansions near Hampden Park to the housing estate of Castlemilk. A relatively affluent and educated seat overall, though with sharp internal contrasts in deprivation.

Name: Glasgow South West
Description: Govan's former shipbuilding heartland, plus the large housing estate of Pollok and the wealthier, highly diverse Pollokshields. Ibrox Stadium and a major hospital now anchor the area's economy, and pockets of affluence and deprivation often sit streets apart.

Name: Glenrothes and Mid Fife
Description: Former Fife coalfield towns along the Rivers Ore and Leven, centred on the mid-century new town of Glenrothes. Coastal communities such as Methil and Buckhaven are among Scotland's more deprived areas, reflecting the decline of mining and heavy industry.

Name: Gloucester
Description: A cathedral city with Roman origins and a historic docks trade, now more reliant on healthcare and public-sector employment. Includes a significant Gujarati Muslim community around Barton and Tredworth, and ranks among England's more deprived seats.

Name: Goole and Pocklington
Description: Combines the inland river port of Goole, historically a hub for shipping, glass and clothing, with the market towns of Pocklington and Howden in the flat, low-lying East Riding countryside. A mixed seat with pockets of low qualification in Goole itself alongside more prosperous rural areas.

Name: Gorton and Denton
Description: Combines diverse, working-class inner-Manchester districts such as Longsight, Gorton and Levenshulme - the latter now home to a large British Asian community - with the more suburban Tameside town of Denton. A young, ethnically mixed and relatively deprived seat.

Name: Gosport
Description: A naval town across the water from Portsmouth, with a strong Royal Navy and defence presence. It combines working-class areas such as Rowner with more affluent seaside communities at Lee-on-Solent and Alverstoke, and has an older population.

Name: Gower
Description: A peninsula west of Swansea and Britain's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, combining the well-to-do coastal village of Mumbles with former mining communities and Swansea's suburbs inland. It has a notably elderly, settled and highly owner-occupied population.

Name: Grantham and Bourne
Description: A predominantly rural constituency centred on the market towns of Grantham and Bourne. Agriculture, food processing and logistics are major employers, with Grantham having a semi-industrial character

Name: Gravesham
Description: A Thames-side Kent seat combining the industrial river town of Gravesend and Northfleet with rural villages such as Meopham towards the North Downs. It has one of the largest Sikh communities of any UK seat, alongside a traditionally working-class, industrial character.

Name: Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes
Description: Reunites the Humber estuary towns of Grimsby and Cleethorpes, once home to the world's largest fishing fleet before its collapse. A working-class seat with one of the highest shares of routine occupations in the country and below-average qualifications.

Name: Great Yarmouth
Description: Centred on the Norfolk port and seaside resort of Great Yarmouth, this working class constituency has very low levels of further education and very high levels of routine employment. Tourism and offshore North Sea Oil and Gas remain important sectors

Name: Halesowen
Description: A Black Country town historically built on nail-making and coal, now largely a Birmingham and Dudley commuter area. It has an average, fairly working-class demographic profile.

Name: Halifax
Description: A West Yorkshire mill town built on the wool trade, with the separate mill town of Sowerby Bridge to its west. A mixed seat with a significant, largely Muslim South Asian population concentrated in its poorer wards alongside more affluent, white areas.

Name: Hamilton and Clyde Valley
Description: Combines the town of Hamilton with rural Clydesdale around Lanark, including New Lanark, a UNESCO World Heritage former mill village. Hamilton itself is a regional hub for retail, local government and higher education, with a more rural, market-town character further south.

Name: Harlow
Description: The New Town of Harlow is characterised by planned neighbourhoods, significant council housing, and a population comprised of working class young families.

Name: Hartlepool
Description: A former shipbuilding and coal-exporting port on the Durham coast, including the resort of Seaton Carew, whose industry has declined sharply since the 1960s. Remaining employers include a nuclear power station and steel tube works, and the seat has a strongly working-class population with low qualification levels.

Name: Harwich and North Essex
Description: Rural constituency centred on theport town of Harwich, alongside Manningtree, Frinton-on-Sea and extensive countryside. The coastal communities have a more retirement-oriented character, while the villages around Colchester have a more commuter character

Name: Havant
Description: Combining the town of Havant and the large post-war council estate of Leigh Park with the seaside communities of Hayling Island and the old fishing village of Emsworth. It has an older, working-class population and one of the region's highest rates of social housing.

Name: Hazel Grove
Description: A commuter suburb on the southeastern edge of Greater Manchester, taking in Marple, Romiley and Bredbury toward the Peak District. Affluent and largely white, with high owner-occupation and a strong contingent of one-person pensioner households.

Name: Hereford and South Herefordshire
Description: A rural, agricultural seat centred on Hereford cathedral city and the market town of Ross-on-Wye, near the Welsh border. It has a notably elderly population and an economy built on cattle farming and orchards.

Name: Hexham
Description: One of the largest constituencies in England, spanning rural Northumberland from Hadrian's Wall country to Kielder Water near the Scottish border. It ranges from the wealthy Newcastle commuter villages of Ponteland and Corbridge to former lead- and coal-mining towns, with a generally affluent, elderly and well-qualified population overall.

Name: Heywood and Middleton North
Description: Two former cotton-mill towns in Rochdale borough, separated by green belt, with the Scout Moor wind farm on the Pennine moors to the north. Contains pockets of real affluence around Norden and Bamford alongside more deprived estates, and lacks tram access despite its Greater Manchester location.

Name: High Peak
Description: Covering much of north-west Derbyshire, the constituency includes the towns of Buxton, Glossop and New Mills. It combines Peak District tourism with former industrial mill towns, many of which have become commuter settlements for Manchester.

Name: Hinckley and Bosworth
Description: A constituency centred on the large market town of Hinckley, alongside villages and the historic Bosworth area. Manufacturing, distribution and logistics remain important employers, while many residents commute to Leicester, Coventry and Birmingham.

Name: Houghton and Sunderland South
Description: Combines former Durham coalfield villages such as Houghton-le-Spring and Hetton-le-Hole with Sunderland suburbs and council estates. It has a strongly white, working-class population, with old mining roots now given over to retail and public-sector work.

Name: Huddersfield
Description: A former textile town in the Pennine foothills, home to a large university and a correspondingly large student population. A working-class, ethnically diverse seat with a significant South Asian and Muslim population, and pockets of high deprivation.

Name: Hyndburn
Description: An East Lancashire mill-town seat centred on Accrington, taking in Oswaldtwistle, Rishton and Great Harwood in the Pennine foothills. Built on textiles and the famous 'Accrington Brick', with a significant Pakistani community concentrated in inner Accrington.

Name: Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West
Description: The former shipbuilding towns of Greenock and Port Glasgow on the Clyde, together with the affluent village of Kilmacolm. Population and industry have declined sharply since the mid-20th century, leaving significant deprivation alongside pockets of wealth.

Name: Inverness, Skye and West Ross-shire
Description: One of the largest constituencies in the UK, spanning the Highlands from Loch Ness and Ben Nevis to the Isle of Skye, with Inverness itself home to over half the electorate. Tourism dominates, from Highland scenery to the Jacobite steam train, and Skye has one of the highest concentrations of Gaelic speakers in the country.

Name: Jarrow and Gateshead East
Description: Covers the shipbuilding town of Jarrow, site of the 1930s Jarrow March against unemployment, together with Hebburn and several Gateshead wards. It has a strongly working-class, largely white population with high levels of social housing.

Name: Keighley and Ilkley
Description: Combines the working-class mill town of Keighley, with its large Muslim population, and the tourist village of Haworth, associated with the Bronte sisters, with the altogether more affluent, middle-class commuter town of Ilkley across Ilkley Moor. A sharply polarised seat, split between old textile heritage and Wharfedale gentility.

Name: Kettering
Description: Centred on the rapidly growing market town of Kettering, this constituency combines expanding suburban housing with surrounding villages. Manufacturing, warehousing and logistics remain important employers, while many residents commute to Northampton, Leicester and London.

Name: Kilmarnock and Loudoun
Description: Centred on the industrial town of Kilmarnock, once known for whisky, carpets and locomotive manufacturing, with the smaller Loudoun towns of Darvel, Newmilns and Galston nearby. A working-class seat that has struggled with industrial decline.

Name: Kingston upon Hull East
Description: Entirely urban, eastern Hull, adjoining the docks along the Humber. A working-class seat with one of the highest shares of routine occupations in the country and very low rates of higher education.

Name: Kingston upon Hull North and Cottingham
Description: Combines middle-class Hull neighbourhoods like the Avenues and Newland, once home to the poet Philip Larkin, with large council estates such as Bransholme and Orchard Park, and the more affluent commuter village of Cottingham. A mixed seat spanning high deprivation and suburban prosperity.

Name: Kingston upon Hull West and Haltemprice
Description: Combines Hull's working-class western wards with the far more affluent East Riding suburbs of Willerby and Kirk Ella. A seat of sharp contrasts, with some of the lowest turnout and qualification levels in the country alongside prosperous commuter villages.

Name: Kingswinford and South Staffordshire
Description: Combining suburban Dudley towns such as Kingswinford with rural South Staffordshire villages including Codsall and Wombourne. It's an affluent, largely retired seat with strong local identities and little in common with nearby Wolverhampton or Dudley.

Name: Knowsley
Description: A Merseyside borough built largely from post-war Liverpool overspill estates around Kirkby, Huyton and Prescot. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, with comparatively high social housing and a notable Safari Park at Knowsley Hall.

Name: Lancaster and Wyre
Description: Combines the university city of Lancaster - liberal and youthful, home to Lancaster Castle and a large student population - with rural, more conservative villages around Garstang in the Wyre valley. Skerton's working-class riverside contrasts with the city's more middle-class core.

Name: Leeds Central and Headingley
Description: Inner-city Leeds around the university and Headingley cricket ground, with the historic ruins of Kirkstall Abbey. Dominated by students, with the highest share of full-time students of any English or Welsh seat, low home ownership and high private renting.

Name: Leeds East
Description: Stretches from the inner-city, working-class Harehills - home to Leeds's largest Muslim population - to suburban estates and commuter villages beyond the M1. A diverse, working-class seat with high deprivation in its inner wards.

Name: Leeds North East
Description: Combines the affluent northern suburbs of Roundhay and Alwoodley, home to much of Leeds's large Jewish community, with the more diverse and working-class Chapel Allerton to the south. A seat of sharp contrasts between prosperous, highly educated wards and areas of high deprivation.

Name: Leeds North West
Description: Affluent north-west Leeds suburbs and market towns including Otley and Guiseley, taking in Leeds Bradford Airport. One of the most prosperous parts of Leeds, with the highest owner-occupation and among the highest qualification levels in the city.

Name: Leeds South
Description: The most working-class of the Leeds seats, covering inner-city Hunslet and Beeston and the council estates of Middleton, home to the world's oldest continuously working railway. A diverse, high-deprivation seat with low home ownership and high social renting.

Name: Leeds South West and Morley
Description: Combines the former mill town of Morley, part of Leeds's 'Heavy Woollen District', with working-class Farnley and Wortley to the west. A middling, mixed seat, neither strongly affluent nor deprived.

Name: Leeds West and Pudsey
Description: Spans working-class inner Leeds around Armley with the more suburban town of Pudsey, historically split between Leeds and Bradford. A seat of sharp internal contrasts in wealth and qualifications.

Name: Leicester East
Description: One of Britain's most ethnically diverse constituencies, centred on eastern Leicester. Highly working class and with the lowest white population in Britain, It has a large Indian population, particularly of Gujarati Hindi heritage, a substantial muslim community, alongside established manufacturing, engineering, retail and service industries.

Name: Leicester West
Description: An urban constituency covering western Leicester, characterised by ethnically diverse neighbourhoods, significant manufacturing heritage and sizeable Black and South Asian communities. It combines residential suburbs with more deprived inner-city areas.

Name: Leigh and Atherton
Description: A flat, former coal-mining and cotton-milling area of Greater Manchester between Manchester and Liverpool, notably lacking a railway station in its largest town, Leigh. Overwhelmingly white, working-class, and below average on qualifications.

Name: Lichfield
Description: A historic cathedral city, birthplace of Samuel Johnson, combined with the former mining town of Burntwood. It's an affluent and largely homogeneous seat, with Burntwood notably more working-class than Lichfield itself.

Name: Lincoln
Description: Centred on the historic cathedral city of Lincoln, this constituency combines a medieval city centre with modern suburbs and surrounding villages. The local economy is driven by public services, higher education, tourism and engineering.

Name: Liverpool Garston
Description: Spans southern Liverpool from affluent Woolton and Allerton to the working-class Speke-Garston estates near the airport, historically cut off from the rest of the city. Home to major Ford/Jaguar Land Rover operations and the Tudor-era Speke Hall.

Name: Liverpool Riverside
Description: Liverpool's city centre and waterfront seat, taking in the regenerated docklands, Anfield and the historic Toxteth/Dingle area. A young, highly educated but sharply unequal seat with a large private-rented population and notably low turnout.

Name: Liverpool Walton
Description: A solidly working-class north Liverpool seat around Aintree racecourse, with extensive terraced housing and long-standing high social housing levels. Historically shaped by sectarian Protestant-Catholic politics, now one of the safest seats in the country.

Name: Liverpool Wavertree
Description: Spans diverse south Liverpool areas from working-class Kensington and Fairfield, home to many non-English speakers, to leafier Aigburth and Childwall, historically home to the city's Jewish community. A young, ethnically diverse seat with a large private-rented population.

Name: Liverpool West Derby
Description: Combines large council estates - Croxteth, Norris Green, Page Moss and Knotty Ash - with private suburban housing around West Derby Village. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, and the filming location of Channel 4's Brookside.

Name: Livingston
Description: A new town seat west of Edinburgh, built from 1962 to absorb overspill from Glasgow and Edinburgh. Retail, logistics and tech employment cluster around the town, alongside former mining and shale-oil communities such as Broxburn and Uphall.

Name: Llanelli
Description: A former industrial town in western Carmarthenshire built on coal, tin and steel, extending into more rural, Welsh-speaking areas inland. It has a working-class character and an elderly population, with owner-occupation well above average.

Name: Lothian East
Description: A rural East Lothian seat running along the coast from Musselburgh to Dunbar. Former mining towns like Prestonpans and Tranent in the west give way to affluent golfing communities around North Berwick, which has some of the highest house prices in Scotland.

Name: Loughborough
Description: A constituency centred on the university town of Loughborough. The presence of Loughborough University gives the seat a large student population, while engineering, manufacturing and logistics remain important to the local economy.

Name: Louth and Horncastle
Description: An rural constituency of market towns, villages and agricultural communities stretching across the Lincolnshire Wolds. Farming, food production and tourism play important roles, while the population is generally older than the national average.

Name: Lowestoft
Description: A coastal constituency centred on the port and seaside town of Lowestoft. Tourism, offshore energy and healthcare are important to the local economy, while the town retains a strong working-class character. Levels of further education and professional employment are very low

Name: Luton North
Description: A densely populated and highly diverse urban constituency covering northern Luton. It has a particularly large Pakistani and Muslim population, with the economy shaped by manufacturing, aviation-related employment, logistics and public services.

Name: Makerfield
Description: A former coal-mining area of Wigan borough, taking in Ashton-in-Makerfield, Hindley and Orrell. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, with below-average qualifications and high rates of routine occupations.

Name: Maldon
Description: A predominantly rural and affluent constituency containing Maldon and rural villages that serve as commuter bases for Chelmsford and South Essex. Home ownership is very high

Name: Manchester Central
Description: Manchester's inner-city core, taking in the city centre, Cheetham (with a large Pakistani community) and areas around the Etihad Stadium, plus Failsworth over the Oldham border. High private renting, low home ownership and a large student population.

Name: Mansfield
Description: A former coal-mining constituency centred on the market town of Mansfield. Although mining has disappeared, the area retains a strong working-class identity, with logistics, manufacturing and retail now among the largest employers.

Name: Merthyr Tydfil and Aberdare
Description: A South Wales valleys seat built on the once-vast Cyfarthfa and Dowlais ironworks, among the largest in the world in the 19th century, and the Cynon Valley town of Aberdare. Now post-industrial, it has low qualification levels and ranks among the more deprived seats in Britain.

Name: Mid and South Pembrokeshire
Description: Wales's south-western tip, taking in the historic port of Milford Haven, Tudor Pembroke and the seaside resort of Tenby, plus St Davids, Britain's smallest city. Known as 'Little England beyond Wales' for its English-speaking character, the area relies on dairy farming, tourism and a major oil and gas terminal.

Name: Mid Cheshire
Description: Centred on the 'salt towns' of Northwich, Winsford and Middlewich, shaped for centuries by salt extraction and the chemical industry it spawned. Includes subsidence lakes known locally as 'flashes', and has more routine occupations and fewer qualifications than surrounding rural Cheshire.

Name: Mid Derbyshire
Description: An affluent mixed suburban and rural constituency covering the Derby suburbs of Oakwood, Spondon and Allestree, as well as commuter villages further to the North, and the ex industrial town of Belper. Owner occupation is very high, whereas social and private renting is very low

Name: Mid Dorset and North Poole
Description: Combining outer suburban Poole and Bournemouth with rural mid-Dorset market towns such as Wareham and Wimborne Minster. A relatively affluent, aging area popular with commuters, and one of the least ethnically diverse constituencies in the country.

Name: Mid Dunbartonshire
Description: Affluent commuter suburbs northwest of Glasgow, including Bearsden, Milngavie and Bishopbriggs, plus more rural villages toward the Campsie Fells. One of the most prosperous and highly educated seats in Scotland, with very little social housing.

Name: Mid Norfolk
Description: A predominantly rural constituency centred on the market town of Dereham Agriculture and food production remain important

Name: Middlesbrough and Thornaby East
Description: Built on iron and steel-making that once drove explosive Victorian growth, Middlesbrough's heavy industry has now almost entirely closed. It is one of the most ethnically diverse and deprived seats in the North East, with a growing minority population in its inner areas.

Name: Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland
Description: Spans suburban south Middlesbrough and the rural Cleveland Hills, taking in the market town of Guisborough and former ironstone-mining villages. It has an older population than the national average and below-average qualifications.

Name: Midlothian
Description: A commuter area south of Edinburgh centred on former mining towns including Dalkeith, Bonnyrigg and Newtongrange. It has grown rapidly with new housing in recent years, and includes pockets of affluence around Roslin, home of the historic Rosslyn Chapel.

Name: Monmouthshire
Description: Wales's most anglicised constituency, bordering England along the Wye Valley and taking in the market towns of Chepstow, Monmouth and Abergavenny. It is affluent and elderly with a professional population, and many residents commute into Bristol and south-west England.

Name: Montgomeryshire and Glyndwr
Description: A large, sparsely populated Mid Wales constituency of small market towns including Newtown, Britain's smallest designated New Town, and Welshpool. Historically among the most agricultural seats in the country, it remains overwhelmingly white and rural, with a settled, owner-occupying population.

Name: Moray West, Nairn and Strathspey
Description: A large, rural seat along the River Spey, taking in Elgin, Nairn and the Cairngorms ski resort of Aviemore. Scotland's whisky country, with distilleries including Glenfiddich and Glenlivet, and RAF Lossiemouth is a major local employer. An elderly, settled population with high home ownership.

Name: Morecambe and Lunesdale
Description: A cross-border seat pairing the seaside resort of Morecambe, with a faded west end and deprived pockets, with rural Lunesdale villages such as Kirkby Lonsdale toward Cumbria. An elderly population, with affluent retirement areas contrasting with genuine seafront deprivation.

Name: Motherwell, Wishaw and Carluke
Description: A North Lanarkshire seat built on the former Ravenscraig steelworks, once one of Europe's largest, alongside the market town of Carluke. Industrial decline has left a still-working-class population with significant social housing.

Name: Na h-Eileanan an Iar
Description: The Outer Hebrides, connected by ferry and causeway across Lewis, Harris and the Uists. It has the highest proportion of Gaelic speakers of any UK constituency, a strong crofting and fishing tradition, and Harris Tweed remains a notable local industry.

Name: Neath and Swansea East
Description: A former coal and metalworking seat centred on the market town of Neath, extending into working-class eastern Swansea suburbs. Industrial decline has left comparatively low qualification levels, though commuter links to Cardiff support relatively strong local earnings.

Name: Newark
Description: A largely rural constituency centred on the historic market town of Newark-on-Trent. Newark itself is semi-industrial and has a sizeable amount of council housing, wheras the rural villages and towns in the constituency along the River Trent are more affluent

Name: Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West
Description: Covers Newcastle's city centre and West End, including the more deprived Benwell and Fenham alongside former mining suburbs further out. It is unusually ethnically diverse and has a large student population for the region.

Name: Newcastle upon Tyne East and Wallsend
Description: Combines the former shipbuilding town of Wallsend with Newcastle's East End, including the Byker Wall estate and more middle-class Heaton. It has some of the highest social housing levels in Newcastle.

Name: Newcastle upon Tyne North
Description: Newcastle's middle-class northern belt, taking in the affluent suburb of Gosforth and the university areas of Jesmond, alongside more working-class Fawdon and Kenton. It has an unusually high graduate population for the region.

Name: Newcastle-under-Lyme
Description: A Staffordshire town historically built on coal, pottery and iron, now anchored by Keele University, with affluent suburbs such as Westlands alongside former mining villages. It has a fairly average, working-class demographic profile.

Name: Newport East
Description: The eastern side of Newport, Wales's third city, taking in the Roman town of Caerleon alongside working-class estates such as Ringland. It has a young population and a notable South Asian community.

Name: Newport West and Islwyn
Description: Combining former mining valleys around Blackwood and Risca with western suburbs of Newport. The valleys area has one of the highest rates of religious non-affiliation in Britain, a legacy of the decline of its once-strong Nonconformist chapel culture.

Name: Newton Abbot
Description: A Devon coastal seat combining the old railway town of Newton Abbot with the seaside towns of Dawlish and Teignmouth and the growing village of Kingsteignton. Tourism and small businesses dominate the local economy, alongside a notably elderly population.

Name: Newton Aycliffe and Spennymoor
Description: A County Durham seat combining the planned New Town of Newton Aycliffe with the market town of Sedgefield, known for its racecourse, and former colliery communities around Spennymoor. It has a strongly white, working-class population.

Name: Normanton and Hemsworth
Description: A West Yorkshire coalfield seat of former mining towns including Hemsworth, Featherstone and South Elmsall, with the larger town of Normanton offering easier commuting to Leeds. A working-class, overwhelmingly white seat with high deprivation.

Name: North Ayrshire and Arran
Description: Combines the Isle of Arran with former industrial coastal towns including Ardrossan, Saltcoats and Kilwinning, once home to shipyards and explosives manufacturing, and the inland Garnock Valley. A working-class seat spanning coast, island and rural upland.

Name: North Cornwall
Description: A long stretch of Cornwall's rugged north coast, taking in Bodmin, Wadebridge and Bude, plus the fishing villages of Padstow and Port Isaac. An elderly, overwhelmingly white seat with little large-scale industry beyond tourism.

Name: North Devon
Description: Covers the 'Golden Coast' beaches around Saunton and Croyde and the towns of Barnstaple and Ilfracombe. A tourism-dependent, elderly and overwhelmingly white seat with a long-standing Liberal tradition.

Name: North Durham
Description: A former coalfield seat between Durham and Tyneside, centred on the commuter town of Chester-le-Street. Its collieries closed by the late 1960s, and employment is now concentrated in retail, health and social care.

Name: North East Cambridgeshire
Description: A rural Fenland constituency where agriculture and food processing dominate the local economy, while the towns contain more economically deprived and working-class communities than much of rural Cambridgeshire.

Name: North East Derbyshire
Description: A constituency of former mining towns, villages and rural communities surrounding Chesterfield. Once dominated by coal mining, the local economy now relies on manufacturing, logistics and commuting to Sheffield and Chesterfield.

Name: North Herefordshire
Description: A rural, agricultural seat around Leominster and Ledbury, the latter known for its cider production, near the Welsh border. It has a notably elderly population and limited public transport.

Name: North Norfolk
Description: Coastal constitueny where Tourism and agriculture are important, while the area has a particularly old and retirement-oriented population, especially along the coast.

Name: North Northumberland
Description: England's northernmost constituency, stretching from the Scottish border at Berwick-upon-Tweed through castle-studded coastline - Bamburgh, Lindisfarne, Alnwick - and Cheviot farmland. It has an elderly, overwhelmingly white population and one of the smallest student populations in the country.

Name: North Shropshire
Description: A remote, rural seat of small market towns including Oswestry and Whitchurch, the latter known for its cheese, near the Welsh border. Farming plays an outsized role in the local economy, and the population is notably elderly.

Name: North Warwickshire and Bedworth
Description: Combining former coal-mining towns such as Polesworth and the working-class town of Bedworth with rural, more affluent commuter villages toward Birmingham. It has a working-class character and below-average qualifications.

Name: North West Leicestershire
Description: A mixed constituency combining former coalfield communities such as Coalville with East Midlands Airport and surrounding rural villages. Distribution, logistics and manufacturing are major employers due to its excellent transport connections between Leicester, Derby and Nottingham.

Name: North West Norfolk
Description: A mixed coastal and rural constituency centred on King's Lynn, the main employment and service centre for western Norfolk. The surrounding area is heavily agricultural, while King's Lynn has a more industrial and working-class character.

Name: Northampton North
Description: Covering Northampton's town centre and suburbs to its north, this constituency combines established residential areas with significant new housing developments. Relative to Northampton South, the constituency is more working class, with significant ethnic minority (including eastern europea) communities, higher levels of social and private renting in the town centre, and low levels of owner occupation

Name: Northampton South
Description: Covering Northampton's 'New Town' southern suburbs, this constituency has a diverse economy based on professional services, retail, logistics and public sector employment. Demographically, it is an average constituency with an above average White-Other population.

Name: Norwich North
Description: Suburban constituency covering northern Norwich and surrounding communities. The souther parts of the constituency are more working class, with extensive council housing, whereas the northern surubs are more middle class with greater owner occupation

Name: Nottingham East
Description: A diverse inner-city constituency covering central and eastern Nottingham. It has a large Pakistani and Black population, a substantial student and young adult population, and a highly urban character, with private renting particularly common.
