The local economy is shaped by education, healthcare, retail and other public and service-sector employment.

Name: Nottingham North and Kimberley
Description: A predominantly working-class constituency combining northern Nottingham neighbourhoods with Kimberley and surrounding former mining communities. It contains some of the city's most economically deprived areas and has a strong tradition of social housing and routine or manual employment, alongside more suburban and owner-occupied communities towards Kimberley.

Name: Nuneaton
Description: A former coalfield town in North Warwickshire, with a large slag heap - locally known as 'Mount Judd' - as a visible legacy of its mining past. It has a mixed, fairly average demographic profile, more affluent to the east than the west.

Name: Oldham East and Saddleworth
Description: Sharply divided between deprived, majority-Asian inner Oldham wards and the affluent Pennine villages of Saddleworth, known for their Whit Friday brass band contests. One of the starkest class and ethnic contrasts of any English seat.

Name: Oldham West, Chadderton and Royton
Description: Takes in western Oldham, the former textile town of Chadderton and Royton, with sharp contrasts between the ex-mill town centre - home to large Bangladeshi and Pakistani communities - and more affluent, largely white outer wards such as Royton North.

Name: Orkney and Shetland
Description: Two remote Scottish archipelagos with a strong Scandinavian heritage, reflected in place names and the Up Helly Aa fire festival. The economy combines fishing, agriculture, tourism and renewable energy, and home ownership is unusually high.

Name: Ossett and Denby Dale
Description: Combines Wakefield's more affluent southern suburbs with the old textile towns of Ossett and Horbury and the rural Pennine villages of Denby Dale and Skelmanthorpe. A comparatively prosperous, older seat for the area, with a strong industrial and mining heritage.

Name: Paisley and Renfrewshire North
Description: Combines the town of Paisley with suburban and rural Renfrewshire around Glasgow Airport, including the more affluent Bridge of Weir. Paisley's industrial and political history runs deep, while deprivation persists in estates such as Ferguslie Park.

Name: Paisley and Renfrewshire South
Description: The southern half of Paisley, once famous worldwide for its textile industry and the Paisley pattern, together with the town of Johnstone. A working-class seat with healthcare, education and Glasgow Airport as major employers.

Name: Pendle and Clitheroe
Description: Combines the former mill towns of Nelson and Colne, the latter with a large Pakistani population, with the market town of Clitheroe and rural Ribble Valley villages beneath Pendle Hill. A historic centre of the Lancashire witch trials.

Name: Penistone and Stocksbridge
Description: Combines Sheffield's northern suburban fringe around Ecclesfield and High Green with the former steel town of Stocksbridge and the rural Pennine market town of Penistone. A comparatively prosperous seat with a strong industrial history but pockets of deprivation.

Name: Penrith and Solway
Description: A vast, sparsely populated Cumbrian seat spanning the Lake District fells, the Solway coast and former coal-mining villages inland from Workington. Elderly, overwhelmingly white and affluent in its rural core, with pockets of post-industrial deprivation nearer the coast.

Name: Perth and Kinross-shire
Description: Scotland's historic former capital, Perth, together with rural Kinross-shire and Highland Perthshire toward Pitlochry. The city itself is socially divided between affluent southern suburbs and more deprived northern estates, while the wider area has a strong hunting, shooting and tourism economy.

Name: Plymouth Moor View
Description: The more working-class, suburban north of Plymouth, dominated by council-built estates and home to Derriford Hospital. Naval and armed-forces employment remains significant nearby.

Name: Plymouth Sutton and Devonport
Description: Central Plymouth, covering the Hoe seafront, the historic naval Dockyards and the city centre, with a very large student population from Plymouth University. Much of the seat was rebuilt after heavy wartime bombing.

Name: Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley
Description: A West Yorkshire coalfield seat combining the historic town of Pontefract, known for its liquorice 'Pontefract cakes', with the former mining and glass-making towns of Castleford and Knottingley. A working-class, overwhelmingly white seat with low qualification levels.

Name: Pontypridd
Description: A South Wales valleys seat combining the former mining town of Pontypridd, birthplace of Tom Jones, with more rural, Vale of Glamorgan-style villages such as Llantrisant. It has a mixed, working-class character and a notable student population around Treforest.

Name: Preston
Description: A former cotton town in Lancashire, now a compact city built around the University of Central Lancashire, with a large South Asian population and newer housing estates at Cottam. Below-average home ownership and a young, ethnically diverse profile.

Name: Rawmarsh and Conisbrough
Description: Former mining communities straddling the Rotherham and Doncaster boroughs, including Rawmarsh, Swinton and Conisbrough, overlooked by Conisbrough Castle and the Wentworth Woodhouse estate. A working-class, overwhelmingly white seat with high social renting and low qualifications.

Name: Rayleigh and Wickford
Description: A prosperous suburban constituency centred on the towns of Rayleigh and Wickford. It has exceptionally high home ownership and a strongly settled character, with very little private or social renting

Name: Redcar
Description: A Teesside seat combining the steel and chemicals town of Redcar with Victorian seaside resorts at Marske and Saltburn, and the ex-industrial Greater Eston area, built around 19th-century ironworks. It has a below-average graduate rate and a strongly white population.

Name: Redditch
Description: A Worcestershire new town expanded rapidly in the 1960s-80s, surrounded by rural villages toward Evesham. It has an average demographic profile and significant commuting to Birmingham.

Name: Rhondda and Ogmore
Description: The classic South Wales mining valleys, including the Rhondda Fawr and Fach and the Ogmore valley, once home to dozens of collieries. It now has low qualification levels, high long-term illness, and one of the highest rates of religious non-affiliation in Britain.

Name: Ribble Valley
Description: A large, rural and affluent seat of Lancashire moorland and the Forest of Bowland, with high owner-occupation and qualifications well above average. Includes the aerospace works at Samlesbury and the town of Bamber Bridge.

Name: Richmond and Northallerton
Description: A large, rural North Yorkshire seat spanning the Yorkshire Dales, the historic town of Richmond and the market town of Northallerton, alongside the huge Catterick army garrison. An affluent, elderly and overwhelmingly white seat reliant on tourism, agriculture and the military.

Name: Rochdale
Description: A Pennine mill town in Greater Manchester, birthplace of the Co-operative Movement, sharply divided between a heavily Asian and Muslim inner core and the almost entirely white, semi-rural Littleborough. Working-class, with low qualifications and incomes.

Name: Rochester and Strood
Description: A historic Medway seat centred on the cathedral city of Rochester, with its Norman castle and strong Charles Dickens associations, alongside Strood and the rural Hoo peninsula. It has a fairly ordinary, working-class character.

Name: Rossendale and Darwen
Description: A chain of former cotton and footwear-manufacturing towns strung along the Rossendale valley - Rawtenstall, Bacup, Waterfoot - together with Darwen. Overwhelmingly white and increasingly a Manchester commuter area via the M66.

Name: Rother Valley
Description: Former mining towns south of Rotherham, including Maltby and Dinnington, alongside more middle-class suburbs such as Wickersley. A working-class seat with high home ownership but below-average qualifications.

Name: Rotherham
Description: An industrial town on the River Don adjoining Sheffield, historically built on steel manufacturing and still associated with metal recycling. A working-class seat with high deprivation and social renting, though the redeveloped Waverley estate has brought a more middle-class population.

Name: Rugby
Description: A Warwickshire railway town, best known for giving its name to the sport developed at its historic public school, surrounded by commuter villages. It has an above-average graduate rate and a fairly affluent, older population.

Name: Runcorn and Helsby
Description: Pairs the post-war new town of Runcorn, with high social housing and a large chemical works, with the far more affluent, largely rural towns of Frodsham and Helsby across sandstone hills to the west. A sharply divided seat either side of the Mersey.

Name: Rutherglen
Description: Blends the Glasgow-adjacent town of Rutherglen with Cambuslang, Blantyre and Bothwell, along the M74 corridor. Once an industrial area of coal, iron and steel, it now relies heavily on commuting into Glasgow, with a sharp contrast between working-class Blantyre and affluent Bothwell and Uddingston.

Name: Salford
Description: Takes in the regenerated MediaCity and Salford Quays waterfront, now home to BBC and ITV studios, alongside older inner-city areas and a historically strong Jewish community around Broughton Park. A young, diverse and heavily private-renting seat.

Name: Scarborough and Whitby
Description: North Yorkshire's coastal seat, combining the traditional seaside resorts of Scarborough and Whitby with rural moorland villages inland. An older, tourism-reliant seat, with a growing potash mine bringing new investment.

Name: Scunthorpe
Description: A North Lincolnshire steel town, built around the Scunthorpe works, with a strongly working-class, industrial character. It has one of the highest shares of manufacturing employment in the country and below-average qualifications.

Name: Sefton Central
Description: An affluent stretch of Sefton borough combining Crosby, Formby and Maghull, with very high home ownership and low social housing. One of the most middle-class Labour-voting seats in the country.

Name: Selby
Description: A North Yorkshire market town with a former coalmining hinterland, taking in the more middle-class Kippax and Methley area near Leeds. A mixed, moderately working-class seat with a strong mining heritage.

Name: Sheffield Brightside and Hillsborough
Description: Covers north Sheffield's inter-war council estates and inner-city Burngreave, plus more mixed Hillsborough. A diverse, high-deprivation seat with England's largest Roma population, concentrated around Page Hall.

Name: Sheffield Heeley
Description: South Sheffield, from the middle-class suburbs of Beauchief and Woodseats to the large post-war council estates of Gleadless Valley and Park Hill. A mixed, moderately working-class seat with a strong tradition of council housing.

Name: Sheffield South East
Description: An eastern strip of Sheffield running from the former steelmaking district of Attercliffe to the ex-mining villages of Mosborough and Beighton, annexed from Derbyshire in 1974. A working-class, ethnically mixed seat with below-average qualifications.

Name: Sherwood Forest
Description: A largely rural and suburban Nottinghamshire, combining rural towns, the Nottingham suburb of Hucknall, and former mining villages. The constituency takes in much of the historic Sherwood Forest area, with tourism and forestry forming part of its identity, while former coalfield communities retain a strong working-class and post-industrial character.

Name: Shipley
Description: Combines the Bradford mill town of Shipley, including the model village of Saltaire, with the more affluent towns of Bingley and Baildon and rural Wharfedale villages. A moderately middle-class seat with a strong textile heritage.

Name: Shrewsbury
Description: A historic market town on the River Severn near the Welsh border, with a well-preserved medieval centre. It has an above-average graduate rate and a notably elderly population.

Name: Sittingbourne and Sheppey
Description: A Kent seat spanning Sittingbourne, once known for brickmaking and paper mills, and the Isle of Sheppey, with the declining dockyard town of Sheerness and the caravan parks of Leysdown-on-Sea. It has a working-class character and below-average qualifications.

Name: Sleaford and North Hykeham
Description: Containing the market town of Sleaford and the Lincoln Suburb of North Hykeham. Agriculture and related industries are central to the local economy, alongside significant military employment connected to RAF bases in Lincolnshire. It has a notably older and settled population, with a large veteran presence compared with many constituencies.

Name: Smethwick
Description: A diverse, working-class Black Country seat with a long industrial history, now dominated by service and healthcare employment. It has substantial White, Asian and Black communities and comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Solihull West and Shirley
Description: An affluent, traditionally Conservative-leaning Birmingham suburb, combining central Solihull with commuter villages and the district of Shirley. It has very high rates of home ownership and professional employment, with a notable Hindu and Sikh community.

Name: South Basildon and East Thurrock
Description: A working-class, Thames-side Essex constituency combining the southern half of Basildon new town with the Thurrock towns of Stanford-le-Hope and Corringham. The economy has shifted from manufacturing to warehousing and logistics around a large Thames-side container port, and the seat has some of the lowest graduate rates in the East of England.

Name: South Dorset
Description: Covers the seaside resort of Weymouth, the Isle of Portland - home to two prisons and a former naval base - and the smaller resort of Swanage. Tourism and quarrying are long-standing local industries, alongside below-average education levels.

Name: South East Cornwall
Description: A rural seat along the Cornish side of the Tamar, taking in the commuter towns of Saltash and Torpoint, opposite Plymouth, and the fishing town of Looe. Notably elderly and overwhelmingly white, with little large-scale industry.

Name: South Holland and The Deepings
Description: A rural Lincolnshire constituency where food production and processing are central to the local economy. Parts of South Holland have also experienced significant migration from Eastern Europe connected to agricultural and food-processing employment.

Name: South Leicestershire
Description: A largely affluent suburban and rural constituency stretching south of Leicester, including towns such as Blaby and Wigston's surrounding communities alongside numerous villages. It has very high levels of owner occupation and a strongly settled, professional character, with many residents commuting into Leicester

Name: South Ribble
Description: Takes in the former Leyland Motors town of Leyland, now largely housing estates, along with Bamber Bridge, Lostock Hall and the flatter farmland around Longton. A settled, largely white, home-owning seat with above-average qualifications.

Name: South Shields
Description: A former shipbuilding and coal-exporting port at the mouth of the Tyne, taking in villages toward Sunderland including the affluent Cleadon and East Boldon, by far the wealthiest part of South Tyneside. Most of the seat remains solidly working-class.

Name: South Shropshire
Description: A large, rural seat of market towns including Ludlow and Bridgnorth, stretching toward the Welsh border amid the Clee Hills. It has a notably elderly population reliant on agriculture and tourism.

Name: South West Devon
Description: Suburban Plymouth commuter territory east of the city, covering Plympton, Plymstock and the growing town of Ivybridge, along with the yachting villages of Newton Ferrers and Noss Mayo. An affluent, elderly and overwhelmingly white seat.

Name: South West Norfolk
Description: A large, sparsely populated West Norfolk constituency spanning the Breckland pine forests around Thetford, fenland around Downham Market, and arable country around Swaffham. Agriculture and a large RAF and army presence give the seat a notably large veteran population and a low rate of higher education.

Name: Southend East and Rochford
Description: Covering the eastern half of Southend-on-Sea together with Rochford and Shoeburyness, this working-class Essex constituency also takes in the isolated, restricted Foulness Island offshore. Graduate levels are below the regional average.

Name: Southend West and Leigh
Description: Covering the more affluent western side of Southend-on-Sea, including Leigh-on-Sea, this Essex seat has a distinctly middle-class, commuter character, and rates of social housing are among the lowest in the East of England.

Name: Southport
Description: A genteel Victorian seaside resort on the Lancashire coast, reluctant to identify with Merseyside, with an elderly population and one of the lowest rates of social housing in the country. Includes flat, rural 'marsh towns' such as Tarleton across the River Douglas.

Name: Spen Valley
Description: A West Yorkshire seat in the old Heavy Woollen District, taking in Heckmondwike, Cleckheaton and the more middle-class town of Mirfield. A mixed, moderately working-class seat with strong local town identities.

Name: St Austell and Newquay
Description: Combines the former china-clay mining town of St Austell, now home to the Eden Project, with the surfing resort of Newquay on Cornwall's north coast, and fishing villages such as Mevagissey to the south. Tourism has largely replaced the area's industrial past.

Name: St Helens North
Description: Takes in St Helens itself along with Rainford, Billinge and Newton-le-Willows, a traditional, largely white working-class seat with an unusually high rate of Christian affiliation. Rainford is a notably affluent commuter suburb within an otherwise industrial seat.

Name: St Helens South and Whiston
Description: Centred on St Helens, historically built on coal mining and Pilkington's glassworks, with Whiston, Prescot and Rainhill to the east. Working-class and overwhelmingly white, with rugby league a strong part of local identity.

Name: St Ives
Description: England's most south-westerly seat, taking in Penzance, Land's End and the Isles of Scilly. Tourism and small businesses dominate a formerly tin-mining economy, alongside significant seasonal deprivation.

Name: Stafford
Description: A Staffordshire county town at the junction of two rivers, with substantial public-sector employment from the county council. It's more middle-class than the surrounding area, with a mix of affluent and working-class suburbs.

Name: Staffordshire Moorlands
Description: A rural upland seat bordering the Peak District, taking in the former textile town of Leek and the Alton Towers theme park. It has a notably elderly, overwhelmingly white population.

Name: Stalybridge and Hyde
Description: A Pennine-edge Tameside seat taking in Stalybridge, Hyde, Dukinfield and Mossley, with a manufacturing past and stone-terraced housing typical of the area. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, with one of Europe's largest floating solar farms on a nearby reservoir.

Name: Stirling and Strathallan
Description: Runs from the Trossachs highlands and Loch Lomond fringe down to the Forth Valley, centred on Stirling, a historic university city dominated by its castle and the Wallace Monument. Tourism is significant, with the Trossachs acting as a gateway to the Highlands.

Name: Stockport
Description: A historic market and mill town straddling the Mersey south of Manchester, mixing affluent northern suburbs like Heaton Moor with more deprived areas such as Brinnington. Once known for silk and hat-making, it retains a well-preserved Georgian and medieval town centre.

Name: Stockton North
Description: Takes in the town of Stockton along with Billingham, once dominated by the Brunner Mond/ICI chemical works, and Norton. It has a working-class character with significant council estates and below-average qualifications.

Name: Stoke-on-Trent Central
Description: The historic heart of the Potteries, once home to Wedgwood and Spode, now one of England's more deprived seats. Graduate rates and professional employment are among the lowest in the country.

Name: Stoke-on-Trent North
Description: Covering two of the historic 'Five Towns' of the Potteries, Burslem and Tunstall, alongside former mining villages toward Kidsgrove. It has a strongly working-class character and low graduate numbers.

Name: Stoke-on-Trent South
Description: Combining working-class Potteries towns such as Longton with the more affluent suburb of Trentham and its historic estate. It has an above-average rate of home ownership for the city.

Name: Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge
Description: An oddly-shaped Staffordshire seat combining the market town of Stone with commuter villages such as Penkridge and former mining communities including Great Wyrley. It has a notably elderly, affluent population.

Name: Stourbridge
Description: A Black Country town historically built on glassmaking, now a mixed commuter and light-industrial seat on the edge of Dudley. It has an average demographic profile, with a notable Bangladeshi community in Lye.

Name: Stretford and Urmston
Description: Takes in Old Trafford, Trafford Park - once Britain's largest industrial estate, now a major logistics and retail hub including the Trafford Centre - and the more residential suburbs of Urmston and Davyhulme. A mixed seat with pockets of real affluence alongside deprived estates like Partington.

Name: Sunderland Central
Description: Covers Sunderland's city centre and coastal suburbs at Roker and Seaburn, once the world's largest shipbuilding town. The university and Nissan's nearby car plant have helped diversify an economy still recovering from industrial decline.

Name: Swansea West
Description: Swansea's city centre and western suburbs, from the well-to-do Uplands and Sketty to more industrial areas like Morriston and Cwmbwrla. It has a large student population and comparatively high levels of social renting.

Name: Tamworth
Description: A Staffordshire town with Anglo-Saxon royal origins, expanded through post-war Birmingham overspill, alongside the wealthy village of Little Aston. It has a working-class character overall, with comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Telford
Description: A Shropshire new town built around the historic ironworking sites of Coalbrookdale and Ironbridge, birthplace of the Industrial Revolution. It has a strongly working-class character with significant council housing.

Name: The Wrekin
Description: Covering the rural fringes of Telford beneath its namesake hill, taking in market towns such as Newport and Shifnal. It combines working-class urban wards with more affluent rural and commuter areas.

Name: Thirsk and Malton
Description: A large, rural North Yorkshire seat of market towns including Thirsk, Malton and Pickering, stretching to the coastal town of Filey. An elderly, agricultural and tourism-reliant seat with modest household incomes despite an affluent appearance.

Name: Thornbury and Yate
Description: A South Gloucestershire seat running from the Severn Estuary through the market town of Thornbury to the former coal-mining, now commuter, town of Yate. It also takes in the more affluent Cotswold town of Chipping Sodbury.

Name: Thurrock
Description: A Thames-side Essex constituency built around the port of Tilbury, the Lakeside shopping centre and the Dartford Crossing, with logistics and warehousing now the dominant local industry. Thurrock has become notably more ethnically diverse than the rest of Essex, with a significant and growing Black population, and some of the cheapest housing in London's commuter belt.

Name: Tipton and Wednesbury
Description: A former Black Country industrial heartland built on coal, iron and steel, now among the most deprived seats in the country. Graduate rates and professional employment are notably low.

Name: Tiverton and Minehead
Description: A large, rural Devon-Somerset seat stretching from the market town of Tiverton, on the River Exe, to the Bristol Channel resort of Minehead, dominated by a large Butlin's holiday camp, and into Exmoor National Park. Notably elderly and overwhelmingly white.

Name: Torbay
Description: Covers the seaside resort towns of Torquay and Paignton on Devon's 'English Riviera'. A largely retired population with below-average professional employment, historically reliant on tourism.

Name: Torfaen
Description: A South Wales valleys seat running from the former mining town of Blaenavon, home to the Big Pit museum, through Pontypool to Cwmbran, Wales's only post-war new town. Once dependent on coal and iron, it now has a working-class, light-manufacturing economy.

Name: Torridge and Tavistock
Description: Devon's largest constituency by area, taking in the port town of Bideford, the market town of Tavistock and much of Dartmoor. Tourism and agriculture dominate a once-industrial economy built on shipbuilding and mining.

Name: Tynemouth
Description: Spans Tyneside's coast from the seaside town of Tynemouth and Whitley Bay through the more industrial North Shields, a former fishing and coal-mining area. It combines affluent coastal wards with pockets of significant deprivation.

Name: Vale of Glamorgan
Description: A mix of farmland and coastline south of Cardiff, centred on the former coal port of Barry alongside the market town of Cowbridge and the Glamorgan Heritage Coast. A large Aston Martin car factory and Cardiff Airport are notable local employers.

Name: Wakefield and Rothwell
Description: Combines Wakefield's cathedral city centre with Outwood and Stanley to the north and Rothwell, separated from Leeds by the M1. A working-class seat with a mining heritage and below-average qualifications, part of Yorkshire's 'Rhubarb Triangle'.

Name: Wallasey
Description: The northeastern corner of the Wirral, facing Liverpool across the Mersey, with a social geography that shifts from grand houses on the upper slopes to working-class terraces in wards like Seacombe. Functions more within Liverpool's orbit than the rest of Wirral.

Name: Walsall and Bloxwich
Description: A working-class Black Country seat combining Walsall, historically known for saddle and leather manufacturing, with the smaller town of Bloxwich. It has a substantial South Asian and Muslim population and comparatively low graduate numbers.

Name: Warrington North
Description: The more working-class half of the Warrington new town, spanning from the industrial core to Birchwood and Culcheth. Below-average qualifications and a strong logistics and distribution-warehouse economy, including large Amazon operations.

Name: Washington and Gateshead South
Description: Centred on Washington, the region's largest New Town and now home to a major Nissan car plant, together with Birtley and Lamesley - the latter home to the Angel of the North. It has a strongly working-class, largely white population.

Name: Wellingborough and Rushden
Description: A mixed constituency centred on the neighbouring towns of Wellingborough and Rushden, combining traditional industrial communities with rapidly expanding housing and logistics development. There is a substantial Eastern European community, while manufacturing, warehousing and distribution remain important sources of employment.

Name: West Bromwich
Description: A Black Country seat spanning several Sandwell towns including Oldbury and Tividale, with a long industrial history now marked by post-industrial decline. It has a diverse population, including substantial Sikh and Muslim communities, and below-average qualifications.

Name: West Dunbartonshire
Description: Runs along the Clyde from Glasgow's edge through Clydebank, once a major shipbuilding and sewing-machine manufacturing town, to Dumbarton and the Vale of Leven. A working-class seat with a significant Catholic population and a strong industrial history.

Name: West Lancashire
Description: Combines the market town of Ormskirk with the New Town of Skelmersdale, built up from 1960s Liverpool overspill and still culturally closer to Merseyside than Lancashire. A largely white, working-class seat with a significant student population around Edge Hill University.

Name: West Worcestershire
Description: An affluent, elderly seat centred on the spa town of Malvern, home to Morgan Motors, and taking in rural villages beneath the Malvern Hills. It has high rates of home ownership and professional employment.

Name: Westmorland and Lonsdale
Description: A large, mountainous seat covering much of the southern Lake District around Windermere and Kendal. Elderly, affluent and dependent on tourism, with a notable EU-born workforce in hospitality.

Name: Weston-super-Mare
Description: A Victorian seaside resort on the Bristol Channel, increasingly a dormitory town for Bristol, with tourism, care work and light industry as main employers. Notably elderly, with the former RAF Locking site now home to a helicopter museum.

Name: Whitehaven and Workington
Description: A West Cumbrian coastal seat combining the former mining and industrial towns of Whitehaven and Workington with Lake District fells inland. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, now heavily reliant on the Sellafield nuclear complex for employment.

Name: Widnes and Halewood
Description: A cross-Mersey seat pairing the former chemical-industry town of Widnes with Halewood, home to a major Jaguar Land Rover car plant. Working-class, overwhelmingly white, and linked by the Mersey Gateway bridge.

Name: Wigan
Description: A former coal-mining town in Greater Manchester, with a strong pub culture and rural, more middle-class fringes toward Standish and Shevington. Overwhelmingly white and working-class, immortalised in George Orwell's 'The Road to Wigan Pier'.

Name: Wirral West
Description: An affluent seat on the western Wirral coast, taking in Hoylake, West Kirby and Heswall, with high owner-occupation and an elderly population. Contrasts with the inland Woodchurch estate, historically one of the area's more deprived communities.

Name: Witham
Description: A rural and market-town Essex constituency centred on Witham and Coggeshall, alongside Tiptree, known for its jam, and the model village of Silver End. The seat combines agriculture with logistics and distribution employment, and has comparatively low levels of both public-sector employment and private renting.

Name: Wolverhampton North East
Description: A working-class Wolverhampton seat of council estates, whiter than the city's other constituencies, extending into more suburban Walsall wards. Graduate rates and professional employment are below average.

Name: Wolverhampton South East
Description: A working-class Black Country seat taking in the former industrial towns of Bilston and Darlaston. It has significant Asian and Black communities and some of the lowest graduate rates in the country.

Name: Wolverhampton West
Description: Combining Wolverhampton's diverse inner-city wards with the affluent, historically separate suburb of Tettenhall. It has a large South Asian population, including a substantial Sikh community, alongside significant deprivation.

Name: Worcester
Description: A cathedral city on the River Severn, historically known for Worcester porcelain and Worcestershire sauce, with a growing university and student population. It has an average, fairly affluent demographic profile.

Name: Worsley and Eccles
Description: Spans affluent Salford suburbs such as Worsley and Boothstown, along with more working-class riverside communities at Irlam and Cadishead on the Manchester Ship Canal. Close to the national average on most measures, with large tracts of green space including Chat Moss.

Name: Wrexham
Description: North Wales's largest town, with a long history of coal, iron and steel, and unusually low Welsh-language use for Wales. Modern employment centres on food manufacturing and light industry, and the town's football club drew global attention after a celebrity takeover.

Name: Wyre Forest
Description: Combining the historic carpet-making town of Kidderminster with Stourport-on-Severn and the affluent market town of Bewdley. It has a notably elderly population and an above-average rate of home ownership.

Name: Ynys Môn
Description: An island constituency off the north Wales coast, taking in the port town of Holyhead and a more Welsh-speaking interior around Llangefni. Tourism, retirement and agriculture dominate the economy following the decline of Amlwch's historic copper mining, and the seat has a notably elderly population.

Name: York Central
Description: York's historic centre and inner suburbs, including council estates at Acomb and Tang Hall, uniquely surrounded on all sides by York Outer. A high-renting, highly studentified seat with a strong tourism and public-sector economy.

Name: York Outer
Description: The suburbs and villages encircling York, including the model village of New Earswick, built for Rowntree's chocolate factory workers. An affluent, highly owner-occupied seat with strong commuter and tourism links to the city.
